# Command-line programs {#sec-cli}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

An R script becomes a command-line program when you run it with `Rscript` and read its arguments with `commandArgs()`. A Rust program is a command-line program from the start: `cargo build` produces an executable, and `std::env::args()` hands it its arguments. This chapter writes the same small tool three ways: in R, in Rust with the standard library's argument handling, and in Rust with the `clap` crate [@clap], which turns a struct into an argument parser with help text and error messages. The tool prints the mean of one column of a CSV file, using the `airquality` data from @sec-io. The matching sections of the Rust book are "Accepting Command Line Arguments" and "Redirecting Errors to Standard Error" [@rustbook, secs. 12.1, 12.6].

## Arguments in R

In R, `commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)` returns the arguments after the script's name as a character vector:

```{.r filename="colmean.R"}
args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)
if (length(args) < 1) {
  message("usage: Rscript colmean.R FILE [COLUMN]")
  quit(status = 1)
}
path <- args[1]
column <- if (length(args) >= 2) args[2] else "Temp"
data <- read.csv(path)
if (!column %in% names(data)) {
  message("no column named ", column)
  quit(status = 1)
}
cat(column, "mean:", mean(data[[column]], na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
```

Run from a terminal, it reads the file and column it's given, or explains how to use it and exits with a status of 1:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
$ Rscript colmean.R data/airquality.csv Ozone
Ozone mean: 42.12931
$ Rscript colmean.R
usage: Rscript colmean.R FILE [COLUMN]
```

## Arguments in Rust

In Rust, `std::env::args()` returns an iterator over the arguments. The first is, by convention, the program's own path, so `skip(1)` drops it, which is what `trailingOnly = TRUE` does in R:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-env-args
#| cargo: true
#| bin: colmean
#| filename: src/main.rs
#| args: [data/airquality.csv, Ozone]
use std::env;
use std::error::Error;
use std::process;

fn column_mean(path: &str, column: &str) -> Result<f64, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut reader = csv::Reader::from_path(path)?;
    let headers = reader.headers()?;
    let index = headers
        .iter()
        .position(|h| h == column)
        .ok_or(format!("no column named {column}"))?;

    let mut values = Vec::new();
    for result in reader.records() {
        let record = result?;
        if let Ok(x) = record[index].parse::<f64>() {
            values.push(x);
        }
    }
    Ok(values.iter().sum::<f64>() / values.len() as f64)
}

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().skip(1).collect();
    if args.is_empty() {
        eprintln!("usage: colmean FILE [COLUMN]");
        process::exit(1);
    }
    let path = &args[0];
    let column = args.get(1).map(|s| s.as_str()).unwrap_or("Temp");

    match column_mean(path, column) {
        Ok(mean) => println!("{column} mean: {mean}"),
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("error: {e}");
            process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}
```

The output starts with the command that ran the program. Running `cargo run` builds the program and then runs it, and everything after `--` is passed to the program as its arguments. To build the tool yourself, make a project with `cargo new colmean` (@sec-setup), whose name the program takes, and add the crates with `cargo add csv` and, for the version below, `cargo add clap --features derive`.

The function `column_mean()` reuses pieces from earlier chapters:

- `position()` returns the index of the first header that matches, as an `Option`, the counterpart of `match(column, names(data))`. Then `ok_or()` turns its `None` into an error message, so `?` can pass it up (@sec-errors).
- `record[index]` is one field of a CSV record. Any field that doesn't parse as a number is skipped. In this file the only such field is `NA`, so the result matches `na.rm = TRUE`. The loop would also skip a stray word silently, though, and keep a field that parses as `NaN`, which `na.rm = TRUE` drops.
- `args.get(1)` returns an `Option` for the second argument, so a missing column falls back to `"Temp"`. Calling `as_str()` borrows the `String` as a `&str`, so both branches have the same type.

Without any arguments, the program explains itself and exits with status 1:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-env-args-none
#| cargo: rerun
#| bin: colmean
#| echo: false
#| error: true
#| args: []
// run again with no arguments
```

Rust's `eprintln!` writes to standard error, as `message()` does in R, so the usage line doesn't end up in a file when a user saves the program's output with `>`. Calling `process::exit(1)` ends the program with a status of 1, like `quit(status = 1)`, and a shell or a CI job can check that status to see that the program failed. A program that ends normally exits with 0.

The program above parses its own arguments, which is fine for one or two of them. Options such as `--column Ozone`, flags in any order, and a `--help` page take a parser.

## Parsing arguments with `clap`

Base R has no argument parser; R scripts that need one use packages such as optparse. In Rust, the usual choice is `clap`. You describe the arguments as a struct, and `#[derive(Parser)]` writes the parser:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-clap
#| cargo: true
#| bin: colmean
#| filename: src/main.rs
#| args: [data/airquality.csv, --column, Ozone, --digits, "3"]
# use std::error::Error;
use clap::Parser;
#
# fn column_mean(path: &str, column: &str) -> Result<f64, Box<dyn Error>> {
#     let mut reader = csv::Reader::from_path(path)?;
#     let headers = reader.headers()?;
#     let index = headers
#         .iter()
#         .position(|h| h == column)
#         .ok_or(format!("no column named {column}"))?;
#     let mut values = Vec::new();
#     for result in reader.records() {
#         let record = result?;
#         if let Ok(x) = record[index].parse::<f64>() {
#             values.push(x);
#         }
#     }
#     Ok(values.iter().sum::<f64>() / values.len() as f64)
# }

/// Print the mean of one column of a CSV file
#[derive(Parser)]
struct Args {
    /// The CSV file to read
    file: String,

    /// The column to average
    #[arg(short, long, default_value = "Temp")]
    column: String,

    /// Decimal places to print
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 2)]
    digits: usize,
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let args = Args::parse();
    let mean = column_mean(&args.file, &args.column)?;
    println!("{} mean: {:.*}", args.column, args.digits, mean);
    Ok(())
}
```

The function `column_mean()` is the same as before. Each field of `Args` is an argument, and its type says how to parse it:

- `file`, with no attribute, is a positional argument, and because it's a `String` rather than an `Option<String>`, it's required.
- `#[arg(short, long)]` makes `column` an option that can be given as `-c Ozone` or `--column Ozone`, named after the field. The `default_value` setting supplies `"Temp"` when it's missing.
- `digits` is a `usize`, so `clap` parses the text into a number and rejects anything that isn't one. Its `default_value_t` setting gives the default as a value of the field's type rather than as text.
- The `///` comments become the help text.

Calling `Args::parse()` reads the program's arguments into an `Args`. In `println!`, `{:.*}` takes the number of decimal places from the argument before the value, here `args.digits`.

The `clap` crate writes the help page from the struct:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-clap-help
#| cargo: rerun
#| bin: colmean
#| echo: false
#| args: [--help]
// run again with --help
```

It also writes the error messages. Leaving out the file name and giving a `--digits` that isn't a number are each reported with a message that names the problem, and the program exits with status 2, the convention for a usage error:

```{rust}
#| label: rust-clap-missing
#| cargo: rerun
#| bin: colmean
#| echo: false
#| error: true
#| args: [--column, Ozone]
// run again without a file
```

```{rust}
#| label: rust-clap-invalid
#| cargo: rerun
#| bin: colmean
#| echo: false
#| error: true
#| args: [data/airquality.csv, --digits, two]
// run again with a bad --digits
```

::: {.callout-note title="An R habit to drop in Rust"}
An R script checks its arguments by hand, if at all: is there one, is it a number, does the file exist? With `clap`, the struct is the specification. Whatever reaches `main()` as an `Args` already has a file name and a `digits` that's a number, so the code after `Args::parse()` doesn't need to check them again. The parser doesn't check that the file exists, though; opening it in `column_mean()` does.
:::

## Building and installing

The command `cargo run` is for development. Running `cargo build --release` builds an optimized program in `target/release/`, and `cargo install --path .` builds one and copies it to `~/.cargo/bin`, which rustup puts on your `PATH` [@rustbook, sec. 14.4]:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cargo install --path .
colmean data/airquality.csv --column Wind
```

An R script needs R, and the right packages, on every machine that runs it. A Rust program compiles to a single executable that runs without Rust installed. It needs the operating system and kind of processor it was built for, in a version no older than the one the build targets.

## Summary

| R | Rust |
|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| `Rscript script.R a b` | `cargo run -- a b`, or the built program |
| `commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)` | `std::env::args().skip(1)` |
| `args[2]` when it might be missing | `args.get(1)`, returning an `Option` |
| `message()` | `eprintln!` |
| `quit(status = 1)` | `std::process::exit(1)`, or `main()` returning `Err` |
| optparse and similar packages | `clap`, with `#[derive(Parser)]` |
| Arguments checked by hand | Arguments checked by their types |
| `--help` written by hand | Help generated from `///` comments |
| A script that needs R installed | A standalone executable |
